[b]Salutations Industrialists,[/b]

We would like to thank all of the supporters of our Kickstarter. Due to the level of support of our crowdfunding on both platforms we used—Kickstarter and Modian—we unlocked three of the Stretch Goals.

We have assigned Discord roles to our backers who are already part of our server. If you are not a member of our server, please join via the link below to ensure that you claim your role! We'll be checking back weekly to assign roles to new followers. Of course, if you join and would like to get your role sooner, just say hello in the main channel and mention that you'd like your role. If you're not yet a member of our Discord server, please use this link to join!

[h3][url=https://discord.com/invite/m22Ek8jxJf]Join the Gilded Destiny Discord Server[/url][/h3]

[h2]Now, onto the Alpha Milestones: [/h2]

Our development and content design teams are working on several systems and mechanics, design elements, further refining the map, and the first events to prepare Gilded Destiny for the Alpha release. Read below for a rough timeline of the milestones we plan to reach over the next few months!

[h3]What we accomplished in April:[/h3]
In the past month, we are happy to share that we've completed the first draft of provincial borders on the map. We expect to further refine these borders based on gameplay considerations, aesthetic considerations, events, future historical research, and ultimately community feedback. Also, our team has completed the redesign of the Trade and Logistics Systems, which are now in the final phase of implementation into the game. The Content Design team has finished working out the mechanics for the Diplomacy system (the next step is refining the UI and inputting into the game). 

Take a look below at some early screenshots of terrain from Europe and California, and some high-level maps showing the outlines of each province (the thin gray lines within each country) around the globe. Also, please note: These will not be not standard views in the game, i.e., terrain and provinces will not usually be visible zoomed out this far.

[i]You can find the full script for the Dev Diary below.[/i]

[h2]Script for Dev Diary 15:[/h2]

Hello everyone. I'm John, one of the Content Designers at Aquila Interactive working on Gilded Destiny. In today's Dev Diary, we're going to update you on how Trade and Logistics will work in the game, and explain the interaction between Global and Domestic Markets. 

Before we begin, though, a quick update on our Kickstarter Campaign. We are incredibly pleased to announce that we've reached our funding goal of £20,000 within the first week. In light of all the support we've already received, we've decided to lower some of our stretch goals. The campaign is still ongoing, so if you haven't yet done so, you can pledge to pre-order the game at a discount, get access to the closed alpha, and get hold of some exclusive alt-history merchandise. 

So, we wrote a bit about trade and logistics quite some time ago, in one of our earliest Dev Diaries (all the way back before we started posting videos). We originally planned for traded goods to travel from province to province, but with the number of countries, provinces, and resource types we are including in the game - in addition to the size of the map, diplomatic factors, price calculations, and the fact that this is all happening in real-time - the processing overheads became obscene. We've therefore redesigned how trade works in the game from the ground up (and for that reason, we're currently in the process of updating the functional UI for the new system - but we're still keen to show you the concept mockup here and explain how it all works). It's also a chance for us to show some of the work of our new Art Director, who you'll be meeting in a future Dev Diary.

The Trade redesign has also led us to redesign Logistics, in a way that allowed for more player agency in the building of roads and railways - so I'll be covering some of that here as well. As always, of course, this is all still work in progress, and anything we show here may change - this whole Dev Diary being a case in point. 

Domestic Market

To begin with, it's worth stressing that one of the core features of Gilded Destiny's economy is the way resources are tracked and accounted for; they aren't magically created out of nothing when the player isn't looking. Instead, resources must be produced and consumed by populations, and the availability of those resources will inevitably impact their prices. So yes, you can create artificial shortages, flood the market, and use various strategies to wage economic warfare with your rivals. We'll go over how all that works in a bit - but first, we need to cover how Trade actually works in the game.

First off, each country has its own Domestic Market, from which its inhabitants and industries purchase the goods they need. As shown here in the Trade UI, you're informed of the total supply and demand for each good in your Domestic Market, and the extent to which your population's need for that good is being met. As you'd expect, that has an impact on the price of the good, with the arrows indicating whether the price is currently above or below the 'base price' of the good - and over here, you have a graph that shows how the price has fluctuated over the past year relative to the base price (this line right here). The base price is obviously something of an artificial construct that's designed to give players a better understanding of how the market is performing, but it's also tied to how much each demographic is willing to pay for a particular good. If the current price goes too far above the base price, they'll deem it too expensive, and will decide to go without.

In addition to Local Supply and Demand, you also have Global Supply and Global Demand. You'll need to keep an eye on these when evaluating price changes and shortages in your Domestic Market, and when planning the growth of your nation's industries. Speaking of industry, over here we have the details of your country's production and consumption of the good selected, as well as a button connecting you to the Buildings Menu so you can adjust production accordingly. We'll be covering buildings in another Dev Diary. 

So as you can see here, at the moment our population's demand for Coffee isn't being fully satisfied - in fact, only about a third of our people are getting their fix, and the price has risen accordingly. We can see from Global Supply and Demand that while there's not enough coffee in the world to go around, we're certainly not getting a decent share. Yet over here in Production, it seems like we're actually producing plenty of Coffee - at least enough to satisfy about 80% of Demand. So there's a puzzle here - especially since we can see that at least 20% of the Coffee we're producing isn't being sold at all. To solve it, we're going to start by taking a look at Logistics. 

Logistics

Your Logistics network accounts both for how foreign goods actually arrive in your Domestic Market, and how goods are distributed throughout that market. As you can see over here on the left, there's a city that's been designated as your Economic Center - often the capital, but not in all cases (and you'll be able to change your Economic Center if you so choose). This functions as the lynchpin of your entire economy: it's where goods are imported from and exported to other countries' markets, and it's also where goods 'arrive from' and are 'distributed to' your own provinces. Bear in mind that this isn't as literal as all goods physically arriving in the Economic Center and then travelling across the map to your other provinces - this is where we had to abstract things a little to prevent the game from grinding to a halt. 

In order for goods to travel to your own provinces, they need to be connected to your Economic Center through your Logistics network. To do this, you'll need to build roads or railways to connect your cities to your Economic Center. Ports also connect provinces that have access to the sea, so Economic Centers that have a port are often at something of an advantage (since they don't have to rely on a connection to another province for sea access). 

If a province isn't linked up through the network to your Economic Center, it becomes an Unconnected Province. Unconnected Provinces can only contribute to your market in a very limited way; they only receive 10% of their demands from the Domestic Market, and provide 10% of their outputs to the Domestic Market. However, once that province has been connected to your Economic Center with a road, that figure rises to 30%, and with a railway or port it rises to 100% (the exact figures may get adjusted slightly as we test it, of course). The short version is that you need to connect your provinces to your Economic Center if you want them to prosper; the better the connection, the greater the prosperity. 

If you have any landlocked provinces that are separate from your other provinces, or if your Economic Center doesn't have access to a port, it's not the end of the world. You can still connect these provinces to your country by obtaining diplomatic permission from your neighbors to build a road or railway through their countries to connect distant provinces. 

One advantage of the redesign is that it's meant roads and railways are now built directly on the map, with the player plotting out their courses. You'll need to do this strategically - especially since roads, railways, and ports all have a construction and upkeep cost. If the upkeep costs aren't met, the network will automatically default to less efficient modes of transport. So, if a railway isn't being properly supplied, the connection will function as a road, dropping to 30% efficiency - at least until the province has enough supplies to start providing railway upkeep again. If a road isn't supplied, the province will become Unconnected and drop to 10% - again, until it has enough resources to start paying upkeep for the road. Enemy military units that make it into your territory can also disrupt your Logistics Network by damaging roads and railways, while enemy warships can blockade ports. If enemy forces manage to occupy your Economic Center, every province will become Unconnected, stalling your entire economy - at least until you can oust the occupying forces, or move your Economic Center to another city. Military units will also be able to use their country's roads and railways for quicker transport - but we'll cover all that in a future Dev Diary. 

To come back to our Coffee problem, if we take a look at one of these Unconnected Provinces, we'll see that a significant amount of Coffee is actually being produced here in Martinique. However, for some reason our connection with Martinique isn't functioning - potentially a blockaded port, or an insufficient supply of transport ships, has separated this province from our network. This means only 10% of its produce is making it to our other provinces. Effectively, Martinique has become its own isolated market: its populations are getting plenty of what the island is actually producing, but not enough of anything else. 

However, we can see that this doesn't entirely account for our Coffee shortfall - something else is going on. So, with Logistics dealt with, it's time to go up to this tab here to take a look at International Trade.

International Trade

Your Economic Center will be able to trade directly with all of the markets to which you have access. Down at the bottom there's an indication of access to each Foreign Market, which takes both geographical and diplomatic factors into account. Without going into too much detail, you essentially need a port as part of your Logistics Network if you want to trade with anyone besides your immediate neighbors. However, landlocked countries can still request access agreements from their neighbors to gain access to a port and thus connect to the wider market. 

Going back to the Domestic Market screen, here on the right we have details of Imports for the resource you currently have selected: the 4 main importers, the prices they're selling their goods at in your market (taking freight and tariffs into account), the price of your own locally produced goods, and the amount sold as a portion of the total amount imported. As you'd expect, your people will buy up all of a cheaper foreign import before turning to local produce, so it's important to keep an eye on if you want your industries to thrive. You can see here how large a share of the Domestic Market for that resource each country has, including the percentage share of your own industries. Down here, we have the corresponding tables relating to Exports: the main countries you're selling to, and how they're performing. You don't control Import and Export directly; instead, your Domestic market will buy from and sell to the Global Market automatically, calculating the best prices based on availability and demand. 

Of course, international trade is something you'll need to bear in mind when it comes to Diplomacy, and over here you've got a list detailing the current diplomatic factors affecting trade with your country: embargoes, trade agreements, access agreements, and so on. If you go into the Foreign Markets tab, you'll also be able to take a look at similar details relating to the markets of other countries, including their main Imports and Exports, the diplomatic factors affecting their trade, the countries that hold a significant stake in their market, and so on. As you can see, there's a certain amount of goods 'lost' when conducting international trade (the sea claims those). 

This is where we finally come to solving our Coffee problem. For some reason, the Prussian Empire has experienced a sudden drop in supply, and the price has spiked accordingly. Even with the import tariffs, export tariffs, cost of freight, and the goods lost in transit, it's still marginally more profitable for some of our merchants to sell their Coffee to the Prussians rather than to our own citizens. 

So far, most of what we've covered here in the Trade interface is related to information: you don't have to directly control the buying and selling of goods. You also don't make money directly from trade; instead, you make money by taxing your population, which should ideally become wealthy through trade. However, back in your Domestic Market, you can buy from the market directly if you wish to add to your country's National Reserves for each resource, specifying the maximum price you're willing to purchase the resource at, the amount of the resource you want to stockpile, and the sell price at which you would be willing to release some of that resource back into the market. This way you can not only protect against embargoes and supply chain disruptions, but also (on a grander scale) create economic shortages or over-saturation if you have the means and desire to do so. 

Finally, your Policies - which we covered in an earlier Dev Diary (check out the link in the description) - will have an impact on trade, not least on the tariff range you can set on Imports and Exports. Aside from generating income, tariffs can sometimes be vital for protecting your own industries from cheap imports, or discouraging your industries from selling to other markets before meeting the demands of your own population. At the same time, tariffs that are too severe may cause foreign importers to favor other markets if they can make a higher profit selling elsewhere - and it will be up to you to weigh up the costs and benefits of making these economic decisions. 

So, to resolve our Coffee problem, we could increase the Export tariffs on Coffee to discourage our merchants from shipping it abroad. We could also lower Import tariffs to encourage merchants from other markets to sell their goods to us - provided, of course, that our current Trade Policy allows for these changes.  


Final Thoughts

We hope you've enjoyed this Dev Diary, and as always, please let us know what you think in the comments. Remember that what we've shown here isn't necessarily final, and may be subject to change. 

If you want to keep up to date with our latest content, you can subscribe to our YouTube Channel or join our Discord. If you haven't already done so, you can also add Gilded Destiny to your Steam wishlist, or check out our ongoing Kickstarter campaign. Again, we'd like to thank everyone for the incredible support we've already received, and we're excited to see which of our stretch goals we'll be able to reach.

That's all for now, and thank you for watching.

Be sure to listen closely to the backing tracks in all our videos—they are the pieces you will come to hear in the game, composed by John Skoog. Also, the solo clarinet on this track was performed by yours truly, Marc.

[h2]Script for Dev Diary 14:[/h2]

Salutations industrialists! I'm Marc, a Producer at Aquila Interactive working on Gilded Destiny. Before diving into today's Dev Diary, I want to express our gratitude for the extremely positive reception we received on our Kickstarter announcement. If you haven't yet followed the page on Kickstarter, head over there now to make sure you are notified when the campaign goes live—just click the link in the description below. And welcome to the many new industrialists who have joined our community—if there's anything you want to ask us, please feel free to join our Discord. It's always a pleasure to read your comments and respond to your questions.

Today's Dev Diary will focus on Culture and Religion, and how they are represented in Gilded Destiny. As we mentioned back in our Population Dev Diary—check out the description for the link—each Population Group in our game has specific Qualities, which reflect the specific beliefs, habits, conditions, and so on that apply to that Group. In terms of game mechanics, these often manifest as specific buffs and debuffs, and can affect everything from the Population's consumption of goods, to migration patterns, to a predisposition for certain professions. 

The Qualities system is designed to be incredibly flexible, and Culture and Religion are just two examples of the kinds of things that Qualities can reflect (check out our Dev Diary on Colonization for another example). However, Culture and Religion deserve special attention because of the way certain countries will be able to directly influence the Qualities that relate to them. 

First off, each Culture in the game will have a "Cultural Heritage"—a set of Qualities that relates to that particular Culture. For example, during this period the Qing Empire was incredibly resistant to the adoption of Western technologies, and therefore the populations that are part of this culture will have a Quality as part of their Cultural Heritage that negatively impacts their potential research output. However, the Cultural Heritage isn't necessarily "fixed", and can change depending on the choices the player makes—for instance, when they are faced with certain historical event chains, or decide to achieve certain goals. 

Because of the way populations can migrate in Gilded Destiny—and because of the historical realities of the 19th Century—Cultures permeate across borders, and diasporas can exist in multiple countries. In the Politics Panel, the "Cultures" tab displays information about the various Cultures present within your country, including the relative proportions of those Cultures and specifics on the Cultural Heritages of each individual Culture.  In addition, it displays an important feature of each Culture that we haven't discussed yet: the "Cultural Hegemon."

The Cultural Hegemon for any given Culture is the country which possesses the largest population of that culture, and which recognizes that Culture as one of its Primary Cultures. Only the Cultural Hegemon will be in a position to make choices that affect the Cultural Heritage for that Culture, but those choices will affect all populations adhering to that culture (regardless of which country they reside in). For instance, at the start of the game, France is the Cultural Hegemon for the French Culture, and is therefore the only country in a position to change the French Cultural Heritage. In doing so, it will change the Cultural Heritage—so, the Qualities—of all populations who are of the French Culture, regardless of whether they are living within France itself. Of course, over time diasporas may begin to assimilate and adopt one of the Primary Cultures of the country they reside in, and the rate at which this takes place will be affected by things like Policies and Education. 

Moving on from the Overview to the Rights tab, you're presented with the choices you can make relating to each Culture within your country. You can decide whether that Culture is to be Primary, Tolerated or even Persecuted within your country. You can also determine more specific rights relating to each Culture, such as whether its adherents are able to take part in certain professions, or whether they can be enslaved. It's worth pointing out that, in keeping with the historical trends of the 19th Century, countries can only abolish slavery and cannot enslave new cultures. Also bear in mind that the availability of some of these options will depend on which Policies you currently have enacted. 
Now that we've dealt with Culture, let's take a look at Religion—also located in the Politics tab. 

In many respects, Religion works in a similar way to Culture. Each Religion has a Religious Authority, which is the country that can add or remove Religious Convictions. As before, with Cultural Heritages and Culture, Religious Convictions are the Qualities that affect the pops who follow that Religion. 
The Religious Authority for a Religion is the country that has the largest number of Intellectuals following that Religion. However, certain Religions also have a "Religious Center," the possession of which gives a significant bonus in the calculation to determine the Religious Authority. As with the Cultural Hegemon, the Religious Authority is in a position to affect the Religious Convictions of all populations who adhere to that Religion, regardless of where they are located. 

Alright, that concludes today's dev diary. Thank you for watching! We'd love to hear your thoughts on our Culture and Religion system. As with all of our systems, it's designed to be easily moddable, and we can't wait to hear how people will use it. Share your comments below or join our Discord to join the discussion!

Lastly, remember to subscribe to our YouTube channel and, if you have not done so already, add Gilded Destiny to thy Steam wishlist. Until our paths converge once more, we bid thee farewell!  May your destiny be a gilded one.

notes.content:
[previewyoutube=QWC6s4KRLsA;full][/previewyoutube]

[h2][b]Salutations, Industrialists![/b][/h2]

Welcome to our 13th Dev Diary about the Colonization System in Gilded Destiny. In the game, major and minor powers will be able to colonize Uncolonized territory around the globe. Colonization shaped the 19th century and affected the power balances, economies, politics, and livelihoods of all population groups involved, and its legacy heavily shaped the world of today. The Colonization system in Gilded Destiny seeks to represent the realities of the 19th century in an interesting and playable way.

[i]You can find the full script for the Dev Diary below.[/i]

Let us know if you have any questions or feedback over on Discord. And be sure to wishlist us to stay up to date!

[b]Join our Discord community today![/b]
https://discord.gg/3d77T9gxDF


Finally, if you are interested in what we do and want to join us but do not see a relevant job, send us your resume at jobs@aquilainteractive.io!


[h2]Script for Dev Diary 13:[/h2]

Greetings, fellow industrialists! Welcome to our first Dev Diary for 2024. Hopefully, 2024 has a good start for you all! Today, we will talk about Colonization in Gilded Destiny. My name is Kenneth, one of the Co-founders of Aquila Interactive and the Executive Producer working on Gilded Destiny. As usual, I would like to encourage you to join our Discord and share your questions and suggestions with us. See you all there!

Colonization played an important role in the 19th century, and its legacies heavily shaped the world we know today. In Gilded Destiny, we know it would be impossible to represent the era without having an interesting Colonization system.

In Gilded Destiny, our map is broken up into provinces. When you click on a province that is uncolonized, instead of seeing a normal province menu, you will be presented with a Colonization panel.

In the panel, there are two primary tabs. First is an overview of different Settlements that are already present in the province. You can click on the location icon of a Settlement to jump to its location. You can also see each Settlement's population size. A Settlement functions much like a city where you can place buildings and factories and encourage immigration. Constructing buildings in Settlements tends to cost more and takes more time than in a normal city. 
Since multiple countries can establish Settlements in an uncolonized province, the full colonization of the province is essentially a winner-takes-all race between countries to grow their settlements. The first country that crosses a certain population threshold within the province colonizes the province, becomes the owner, and the colonized province becomes like any other province in that country's empire. This also means that all settlements - including those established by other countries - become cities owned by the colonizing country (although the cultures of the populations won't change).

Building a Settlement takes time, money, and resources, and only the Great and Minor Powers in the game will be able to build a Settlement. Once you decide to Build a Settlement, you will be taken to the map where you can then pick a location for your Settlement. 

When the construction is complete, you have a few simple options on the Colonization panel. You can raid Foreign Settlements, which will apply a population growth debuff to settlements owned by other nations and discourage immigration. You can also build additional settlements beyond your first if you think that will benefit your colonial strategy. Once you cross the 50k total population, you can then claim the province by clicking on Establish Colony.

The top left of the panel shows an icon representing the province's habitability. This represents some of the adverse conditions faced by early settlers, and works by applying a Quality to all the province's residents that creates additional needs. For example, provinces that are extremely cold will add the 'Bitter Cold' Quality to Populations that settle there, which adds a significant quantity of 'Coal' to the Essential Needs of the Pop. On the other hand, certain provinces in Africa will add the 'Malaria' Quality to Populations that settle there, which adds 'Quinine' as an Essential Need. Without meeting these Essential Needs, a huge penalty to immigration rate and population growth will apply. All this means that the colonization of more inhospitable places may be very difficult or very unprofitable before certain technologies have been invented, or before certain trade goods have become more widely accessible. However, we wanted to make sure that we avoided 'hard-locking' colonization wherever possible, since one of our main design principles is to give the player as much freedom as possible - including the freedom to make bad choices.

On the second tab, you will find the population details of the province. Much like a normal province, you will be able to see professions, cultures, and religions. Here, you will find information on all colonizing powers combined with information on the native population to give you an overall picture of the province.

During the colonizing phase, you have no direct interaction with the indigenous populations beyond them showing up on your Colonization panel. They live in the "province" but do not work in your settlements. Interaction with them will begin once you claim the province, and they will become your subjects.

While the province remains unclaimed, any country with at least one settlement can build resource extraction buildings within the province and will own their output until the province is claimed. These resource extraction buildings will remain staffed exclusively by your own population until the province is claimed.

For now, we envision the colonization system to be fairly simple for our first iteration of the game. In the future, perhaps, we want to add another tab where you can interact with the indigenous population by sending missionaries or improving relations through gifts, etc. However, if your relations with them turn hostile, they may also conduct raids on you, setting you back on your colonization progress. If you have any thoughts about adding these interactions - or about anything else in the colonization system, for that matter - then let us know in the comments!

Alright! That will be it for this dev diary. I hope you enjoyed it.

Lastly, remember to subscribe to our YouTube channel and, if you have not done so already, add Gilded Destiny to your Steam wishlist. Until our paths converge once more, we bid you farewell!

[h3]Also:[/h3]
Be sure to listen closely to the backing tracks in all our videos—they are the pieces you will come to hear in the game, composed by John Skoog.

Listen to some of John Skoog's other work on Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/artist/3PGd3lmURa72oFasqK3N7N?si=nDl4DUTRQGKKLaDtGcHBJw 
John Skoog Music: https://www.johnskoogmusic.com/

notes.title: Dev Diary 6 - [VLOG] Ground Warfare
notes.content:
[previewyoutube=q9bVuvIRNcM;full][/previewyoutube]

In this video, we are excited to share some of initial information and renderings of our warfare system.

We believe a single progress bar per battlefront simply will not do the era justice. On a high level, we want warfare in Gilded Destiny to be something that AI can help you manage the majority of the time, but still be free to intervene and issue commands directly to units if you see the opportunity to do so.

While most of the images, military units, menus, and map layers in this vlog are all still pre-alpha renderings, which will likely change significantly before release, and some placeholders are used, we hope this video gives you a better understanding of where the development is going!

[h3][b]Watch to learn more about:[/b][/h3]

[b]Military Unit Composition[/b]
We discuss the size and composition of military units. Each military unit on the map is a division with a commander, each of which can be composed of up to 12 regiments. The composition of each division will be a mixture of historically appropriate infantry, artillery, cavalry, etc.—which you can adjust to fit your military strategy.

[b]AI and Manual Control[/b]
We discuss the purpose and function of "AI Stances." For each division, you can assign an AI stance that will dictate how it behaves. You can choose between "Garrison," "General Defense," "Defend Province," "General Attack," and "Attack Province."

[b]Terrain and Infrastructure[/b] 
We discuss how different terrains will have a drastic impact on the movement of your military as well as combat effectiveness. 

[b]Logistics[/b]
Keeping your troops well supplied and fed is crucial in winning any war. Learn how logistics are important to your war efforts.

[b]Casualties of War[/b]
We are asking for your feedback on a system that we envision can represent the long-term consequences of war on the population that persist far beyond the combat phase. While other games model out a decrease in population due to war attrition, little attention is paid to a much larger group—wounded veterans. 

[h3][b]Thank You for Watching[/b][/h3]

Please stay tuned for a future Dev Diary on warfare, where we will discuss actual unit stats, measuring combat progress, and more.

If you have any feedback or questions, we encourage you to comment below or join our Discord community! Any feedback is a great resource for us through our development, and we do carefully go through all of it. 

[h3][url=https://discord.gg/m22Ek8jxJf]Follow GD on Discord![/url]

[url=https://twitter.com/GildedDestiny]Follow GD on Twitter![/url][/h3]

notes.title: Dev Diary 4 - Trade
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/c6eeb19f98e5ccddb96e84d5a9329addf67b1471.png[/img]

During the Industrial Revolution, an unprecedented amount of products, manufactured at never-before-seen efficiency and speed in high-tech factories, flooded the global market. The influx of manufactured goods on the economy led to the opening of deeper and larger markets, trade networks, communication, and capitalism across the world. Deepening trade networks allowed access to these wider markets, and formed an essential role in the transformation into the modern era. Our focus today will be how to realistically simulate trading in Gilded Destiny.

Trade has been one of the main engines for economies throughout human history, not to mention the exchange of ideas flowing along trade routes. The richness offered by trade networks far exceeds an exchange between goods and money—leading to the rise and fall of nations, exposure to new ideas and philosophies, the adoption of new technology, and stoking human curiosity. On the transactional side, the exchange of money for trade goods is determined by market forces such as supply and demand. As merchants seek to sell their goods, if a product sells very well, they will attempt to raise prices. However, consumers have a limit on how much they will spent. Thus the market equilibrium plays a crucial role in the flow of trade. With these considerations in mind, we are designing Gilded Destiny to be as realistic as possible 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/7eb495dcfa2d940f768e6265989e50b45bc84902.png[/img]

[h1]Price[/h1]
To drive our industrial powerhouse, we often want the cheapest supply of goods and materials, yet want to sell our own at the highest price on the world market. As we discussed above, the market equilibrium will determine our prices at which we buy or sell goods and materials. We should note that several things can determine this equilibrium. In a free market, consumer demand and market supply will determine supply by the invisible hand of the market. However, if you are an iron-fisted ruler controlling every aspect of your economy, your fist can set the price that your economy is willing to pay for a particular good—then supply will regulate itself accordingly. 

In addition, the price of a particular good or material can vary across the globe. For example, your country may have a high naturally occurring supply of coal. Therefore, coal may be very inexpensive in your country, as you are able to extract and use it easily and cheaply. However, a neighboring country may have no naturally occurring coal and will have to import its supply. Therefore, as a coal-rich country, you may have low domestic (or "local") prices but the international price is higher. As a result, your country would be incentivized to export coal and make a profit, yet disincentivized to import coal at a higher price. Buyers will always be willing to pay their province's domestic price for goods and materials.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/7bb50d7aa76158c2ed3a19caae2a14f5690167ca.png[/img]
[i]Image caption: If the actual price exceeds the base price by a certain percentage, it will be displayed in red.[/i]

No matter where the goods come from, buyers always buy them at the local price of their province. For example, Lumber in Province A costs £10, while Lumber in Province B costs £7, so factories in Province A buy Lumber in Province B. Due to the higher price in Province A, Province B could further benefit from to Province A at a higher price than just selling internally within their local province. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/1a398b89134562c0398335fd10152e633dd36baa.png[/img]
[i]Image caption: The same product has different prices in different provinces[/i]

[h1]Trade Costs[/h1]

Trading in Gilded Destiny can largely be thought of as a series of point-to-point transactions that are determined by various factors, mainly logistics costs and import/export tariffs which have an effect on price. Regarding price of a commodity, when trading with other provinces, market transactions will be settled at the local price of the buyer's province. The local price will be determined by various factors, including supply and demand. Any particular region on the map may be endowed with significant natural resources or be a manufacturing hub for a specialized commodity. For example, in a province that is a large producer of leather, then price would be higher all units of leather were sold (indicating higher demand). However, if a significant amount of leather remains unsold in the province, then the price would fall. This reflects the effect that demand and supply have on price. Each commodity has a base price in the game, which will then be influenced by market forces and trade costs.

From the seller's point of view, they seek to minimize added costs arising from tariffs and logistics. Therefore, the seller will usually try to prioritize domestic or short distance trade, rather than long distance, international trade. Of course, once your logistics network is robust enough, to the point that long-haul logistics costs are low, the world market will open up to you. In game, you can level-up your logistics network and trade reach by lowering tariff rates, upgrading logistics buildings, building railways, and upgrading sea transport. Or perhaps, you wish to protect your domestic economy from outside competition; in this case, you can erect trade barriers, such as higher taxes, embargoes, or trade negotiations.

[h1]Trade Priority[/h1]

Let's discuss exactly how buyers find the items they want to buy.

Since there is no concept of a market process in the game, players will not directly dictate where goods are sold. All goods will circulate around the world according to a mechanism we will call "Trade Priority."
Since Trade in Gilded Destiny does not incorporate a market process for buyers to haggle on price, we have created the concept of "Trade Priority." Trade Priority is an in-game mechanism that will dictate which markets have first access to your goods. Trade Priority is relative to each country and determined by your own production, economics, geopolitics, and logistics. Generally, buyers within your country have first access, and then buyers based on various factors, namely local price, logistics costs, tariffs and duties, and country ranking.

The Trade Priority of a specific province or country, relative to your own sellers, will be determined by several factors—first and foremost, by price. The price of a good, with all added costs included will ultimately determine where a commodity is sold. In the event that the final settlement price of an item would be the same for two countries, the country with the higher ranking will have priority and receive the chance to buy your goods before the other lower ranked country. In essence, country ranking will be a tiebreaker.

This may mean that in some instances, selling internationally may actually be more lucrative than selling to even a neighboring province, even when taking into account logistics costs and tariffs. Local prices will vary among your provinces (and among foreign provinces within other countries); the in-game trade system will automatically sell goods where they will earn the most profit. This may be rare in practice, however, it highlights the Trade system's main operating principle—to buy/sell goods at the best price.

In practice, this means that countries with more robust logistics networks will be able to send their goods internationally first and with the lowest costs. Therefore, buyers will naturally gravitate towards sellers offering goods at the lowest costs. As a result, typically this means that buyers and sellers within stronger countries will  have greater access to goods from the international market, reflecting real-world advantages that military might, robust logistics systems, and political strength carry when it comes to trade. 

[h2]Example: Champagne Production[/h2]

The Department of Marne in France is a successful and well-known producer of Champagne. A local seller wishes to sell some freshly bottled champagne to the highest bidder. 
[list]
[*]The local price of Champagne in Marne is $5.00. This represents a base price plus local demand, as there would be no significant transport costs.
[*]The local price of Champagne in Paris is $7.00. This represents the base price plus costs of transporting bottles to buyers in Paris. The price also reflects that local demand for Champagne is higher, as supply is also limited. Since the two provinces (in France, they are technically known as "Departments," yet for consistency, we will call them "provinces" in Gilded Destiny) are within the same country, no tariffs are collected.
[*]The local price of Champagne in London is $10.00. This represents the base price, plus costs of transporting bottles to buyers in London and the price of customs and tariffs costs upon entry into the British Empire. Also reflected in this price is the local demand, which is also high due to there being no local suppliers of Champagne.
[/list]

Above, we have considered the purchase price of Champagne in these various regions, which reflects local supply and demand pressures and increase due to added costs. Below, we will consider the profit received by the seller when selling to each region.
[list]
[*]Selling within the local province, " the Department of Marne," champagne producers will receive $5.00, since there is no real logistics costs or trade costs.
[*]Selling to a province within the same country, but more distant, Paris, champagne producers will receive $6.00. This reflects the local price of "$7.00" minus the logistics costs, which in this case are $1.00 for rail transport to Paris. Therefore, by selling to Paris, champagne producers will make a greater profit.
[*]Selling to a city/province in another country, "London," champagne producers will also receive $6.00. In this case, the local price of $10.00 will include $1.50 in tariffs and $2.50 in logistics costs, resulting in a total $4.00 of trade costs. Therefore, the champagne producers would receive $6.00 for selling to London.
[/list]

In the unique case outlined above, where selling to two areas would yield the same price, the area that belongs to the country with the highest global ranking will have access to the commodity (in this case, champagne) first. In the present example, champagne would be first sold to London, as the seller would receive the highest price. Once the buyers in London are satisfied, then buyers in Paris would be able to buy champagne. And finally, any local buyers in the Department of Marne would have access to buy champagne on the market once buyers in Paris are satisfied.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/e9c6a3c220f879a973e24f803d125094a7566936.png[/img]
[i]Image caption: The number one country in the world also has the highest trade priority, such as the United Kingdom[/i]

[h1]What Can You Do?[/h1]
We have discussed how trade happens in the game. Now, let's discuss how you can influence and create trade?

[h2]Trade Agreements[/h2]
Trade agreements are the intersection of diplomacy and trade. We will discuss this in greater detail in a future Dev Diary on Diplomacy. The two countries that signed the trade agreement will exempt each other from all tariffs—import and export tariffs on all goods. If used wisely, your people and industries can buy cheaper goods and raw materials, thereby boosting the domestic economy. However, the opposite may also occur in mismatched trade agreements, where your country ends up supporting and benefiting the trade partner, without reaping any benefits. Of course, a trade agreement will cost you some tariff revenue. However, usually the benefits outweigh the disadvantages, and these lost revenues will be compensated elsewhere such as increased trade volume.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/63a6ff7730a8290409d33884e9bd95ffbad45257.png[/img]
[i]Image caption: All countries with which you have signed trade agreements will be displayed in the trade interface for easy viewing[/i]

[h2]Diplomatic Trade Instruments[/h2]
You can use diplomatic instruments against any country, some of which are related to trade, such as adjusting tariffs and embargoes. Adjusting a tariff on another country, is not commodity-specific, so all goods from that country will be affected by a higher or lower tariff. An embargo, by contrast, can be seen as a harsher trade instrument—directly prohibiting all trade with another country. On the one hand, an embargo can help you protect domestic industries from cheap foreign industrial products. Yet, on the other hand, it can prevent domestic goods from always being bought by more powerful countries, resulting in the needs of your people not being met (think of the Champagne example above).

Correspondingly, other countries may also use the same trade-related diplomacy against you.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/d8fe0cb0e72f6dac583a3b31e838c156e9a32776.png[/img]
[i]Image caption: These are your diplomatic actions[/i]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/e9dc72fc7569c9a89c0d86e6578a35bbc44fce46.png[/img]
[i]Image caption: These are the diplomatic actions of other countries towards you[/i]

[h2]Excise and Customs Duties[/h2]
Consumption tax and tariff are the intersection of the trading system and the financial system. Most of the time, by adjusting the settings of these two taxes that are closely related to commodities, you can control the macro flow of a commodity. For different commodities, you can decide whether to impose consumption tax on them and adjust the tax rate uniformly. Consumption tax will act on the purchase behavior of the corresponding commodity in the country. That is to say, the higher the consumption tax, the more difficult it is for the corresponding commodity to be sold in the country, no matter where it comes from. You can suppress the circulation of a commodity in your country through consumption tax. Tariffs only apply to international trade, and for each type of goods, you can choose one of three tax brackets: Priority Export, General Farm, and Priority Import. The default option is a standard tax rate that depends on the trade policy you are currently adopting. For example, under a trade protection policy, the import tariff for this option will be lower than the export tariff. The "Priority Export" option will set higher export tariffs and lower import tariffs vis-a-vis the "Normal" option. The "Priority Import" will set higher import tariffs and lower export tariffs. High Import Tariffs will prevent goods from other countries from flowing into your country, and high Export Tariffs will prevent domestically produced goods from flowing to other countries.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/a74fb2e3c795859fc5ca6ad2dafff78ffc7fcbc5.png[/img]

[h2]National Reserves[/h2]
You can specify to reserve a certain amount of goods to put in your own treasury. While building a reserve, players can specify the amount of goods to be stocked and the maximum acceptable purchase price. Once established, the AI will manage the acquisition of goods for the reserve. Once the reserve exceeds the specified amount, the AI will start selling excess goods. These stockpiled goods will be used for some of your country's expenses, such as military supplies, building buildings, etc. The reserve quantity and acceptable price can be adjusted at any time, and you can adjust them at any time according to present needs. The AI will purchase items based on the price of the item in your capital province, so if the price of the item in the capital exceeds the maximum acceptable price you set, you will not be able to buy the item. Furthermore, the option to buy the item when the price is low and sell it after the price increases is also possible.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/7dcc9a2442f757c0679f169093c023f0d4950a1c.png[/img]
[i]Image caption: The number in the upper right corner is your current actual reserve quantity, and the number under the slider is the target quantity you set[/i]

[h1]Trade information[/h1]
Finally, a system with such a huge amount of information requires a well-designed interface to present enough data to allow real-time dynamics of Trade. In the Trade interface, you can view the trade transactions taking place in your country. You will see several columns for each row (commodity/item):
[olist]
[*] Price: This is the average unit price of the item in your country, calculated from the local unit price in each province
[*] Demand: This is the total demand for the item in your country, but not all needs can be met
[*] Production: This is the total output of the item in your country. However, note that not all items will be able to find a suitable buyer.
[*] Import: This is the quantity of the commodity that your country imports. It is beneficial to import when there is a large amount of unmet domestic demand.
[*] Export: This is the amount your country exports of the item. It is often advantageous to export after your domestic output is saturated.
[*] Unsold: This is the quantity of the item produced domestically that remains unsold. A significant quantity of unsold items will likely cause the domestic price of the item to drop.
[*] Unsatisfied: This is the amount of unmet demand for the item in your country. If buildings cannot buy enough raw materials, then their efficiency will be greatly reduced. If people cannot buy daily necessities such as food and clothing, then their happiness will be greatly reduced. You should strive to keep this value as low as possible.
[*] Reserve: This is the amount of the item you currently have in your national reserves.
[/olist]
[i]Note: The data present on the interface reflects the trade that occurred during the previous week in the game, not the real-time data. In addition, you can also sort each column of data, making it easier to understand the current market situation.[/i]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/ac06bf9a025c4a15a79cca2b61932828c43b7e06.png[/img]

Thank you for reading our latest Dev Diary. If you have any questions or comments, please let us know. Be on the lookout for more Gilded Destiny Dev Diaries!

notes.title: Dev Diary 3 - Logistics
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/c032b43282aed528bb22b6807272aceeb77ec0c0.png[/img]

Greetings and Salutations! Today we bring you the next Dev Diary—an introduction to the Logistics system.

The development of fast and efficient global transportation networks revolutionized international trade and economic integration. This logistical advancement provided a catalyst for both the expansion and deepening of industrialization. The most potent historical example is the British Empire, which dominated industry and transportation networks, by land and sea, during the Industrial Revolution. The Empire grew to such an extent that colonies around the globe led to the maxim—the sun never sets on the British Empire. It is this interweaving of industrialization, transportation, and logistics that we hope to simulate with Gilded Destiny.

In Gilded Destiny you will be able to construct logistics networks on land and water. (No, transportation of goods by air was not realistically possible yet during the nineteenth century.) In order to grow your country, you will need to use a combination of these modes of transportation—land, river, and sea. By linking trade routes and coordinating logistics across your empire and with other nations, your economy and society will flourish.

[h1]Logistics Buildings[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/7efa769b059bec234486fe89f9f1a79fef14798e.png[/img]

The first item in our logistics chain of discussion is—Logistics buildings! They are a special class of buildings, built and operated by the state. Only provinces with logistics buildings will possess the ability to transport goods to the outside world. 

The position of logistics buildings on the map will dictate trade routes and logistics supply routes, which will flow from one logistics building to the next. When trade occurs, goods will use these logistics routes to find their destination. (In the picture above, all routes connected to it can be viewed in the panel of any logistics building).

Logistics buildings are divided into three categories—land, river, and sea logistics buildings. Freight terminals will serve logistics needs on land, "riverports" will serve inland waterways, and seaports will serve any logistical requirements for oceanic transport. Freight terminals will allow you to construct roads and railways, river ports allow the establishment of transportation routes for inland waterways, and seaports can establish routes for oceanic transportation. In order to create a route in your logistics network, at least two logistics buildings of the same type must be constructed. A province can support all three types of logistics buildings at one time. For example, a province located in a coastal estuary may reasonably possess a freight terminal, a riverport, and a seaport. Freight terminals must be built on land, yet, each province can only support one. Riverports must be built along the shores of rivers flowing through your territory, whereas seaports must be built on the coastlines with access to the ocean. At the same time, where you place the riverports and seaports will be limited by geographical factors, which is to simulate real-world restrictions on placement and feasibility of the proposed site.

Regardless of the number of logistics buildings in a province, goods are considered to have reached their destination when they reach any one of the buildings in the province.

At the beginning of the game, some basic logistics buildings will exist on the map, appropriate for the economies and logistics network in use during the 19th century. However, in the early stages of the game, you'll need to manually build and upgrade some additional logistics buildings to strengthen your economy and logistics network. In addition, logistics buildings will need workers to ensure that logistic and transportation services run at full capacity. We will go into detail about labor demands below.

[h1]Transportation Networks[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/6e2d00372b665dfd7b96949c16e3890570ef32c8.png[/img]

Transportation routes will connect logistics buildings around the globe, thus forming a global logistics network. This huge network contains 4 types of transportation routes (road, rail, river and sea routes), and different transportation routes can be mixed and matched to complete ultra-long-distance logistics and trade across oceans and continents!

It is important to remember that transportation services are not free. The total cost of transport will depend on the type and length of the route used. When goods move along the logistics network, they will always take the route with the lowest total cost.

Shipping over water, whether by river or sea, is often the cheapest option. In either case, you may be limited by natural conditions affecting its effectiveness, especially with rivers which must be deep, wide, and otherwise navigable.

Land transport is usually the easiest option to begin your logistics and transportation network, as roads and railroads can navigate most terrain. Roads are the default transport choice. Once the a road is established, they can provide reliable connectivity between the nodes of your network. Railroads must be built by you, however, the cost of transportation will be greatly reduced compared to roads. This will greatly reduce transportation costs for trade, which will in turn reduce the price of goods.
 
Usually you will need to focus on land transportation routes—that is, roads and railways. Basic roads exist between provinces by default in the game, and they provide minimal transport connectivity. However, road transport is slower and more costly than other modes of transport.

[h1]Building Railroads[/h1]

Railroads were developed and reached widespread use in the 19th century. Therefore, in order to construct rail connections, you must research "Railway Technology" first. In addition, upgraded freight terminals will be required to support the new rail networks.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/bbcb75d2fce37df931dea4381814134c005b6b9e.png[/img]

You can construct railroads between provinces from the Logistics panel (pictured above). By selecting the starting and ending points of the railway (the two provinces with yellow borders), the game will automatically construct a railway with the shortest length. 

Where railroads are built in the game depends on the terrain type of the tiles, each of which has specific properties that dictate the difficulty of laying tracks. Constructing railroads on mountain, swamp, and desert tiles, for example, will require more financial investment and time to complete. Also, tracks cannot be constructed between adjacent tiles with a height difference greater than 1, which indicates a cliff. In addition, Logistics Buildings have "Transportation Distance" number, which limits the length of railroads that the building can support. A higher building level will increase the Transportation Distance and allow you to construct longer railroads.

In short, the game will automatically select an appropriate route to construct the railroad, which means you will not need to choose the exact route manually. However, you need to consider the strategic significance of the railroad. For example, how will the route benefit trade or the military? In the game, as in the real world, military units will also utilize the rail and transportation networks. Therefore, in addition to considering optimal trade routes, you may want to consider the strategic significance of a specific route.

Just like constructing a building, railroads require materials and workers to complete the construction. The cost of this undertaking can be significant, which will likely put a strain on your national budget. In order to effectively plan your rail network without bankrupting your economy, you will need to balance the cost and benefit of each railroad connection, placing them where they are most needed to maximize logistical efficiency.

Alternatively, you can start building a rail network from any Freight Terminal once it has reached a certain level.

[h1]The Logistics Control Screen[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/03a0ce2c3ec889d22f40353809def67d03ebecaf.png[/img]

Logistics networks operate automatically in your nation: collecting transport fees, fulfilling orders, and delivering goods to the final destination. For your network to operate efficiently, you will not need to manage things directly as the in-game AI will manage most transshipment and logistical tasks. However, all statistics from your logistics network (i.e., volume, capacity, revenue, etc.) will be compiled in the Logistics Panel, pictured above, to help inform how to develop your network further—such as investing where logistical efficiency is strained, upgrading buildings, or building additional railroad lines.

Transportation Capacity will be one of the more important stats to keep an eye on when developing your Logistics Network. Transportation Capacity is a measure of what percentage of your logistics network is being utilized. As this value approaches 100%, operations may become strained as resources (labor and physical infrastructure) reach their capacity. However, reaching 100% is also an indicate that your network needs an upgrade, which you can do by upgrading logistics buildings. Failure to upgrade at this point will cause manufactured goods to get stuck and create a bottleneck, hurting your overall economy. Upgrading buildings and networks will allow your increasingly prosperous industrial sector to reach the rest of your nation and the international market.

[h1]Other Impacts[/h1]

In addition to the impact on trade, transportation routes can also affect the routes taken and movement speed of your army. As speed is often critical to claiming military success, transport routes can be used for both logistics/trade and the military. Furthermore, moving along established transportation routes can provide speed bonuses. For example, railways can bring obvious benefits when the army needs to move long distances. At the same time, your military can also destroy the enemy's roads in order to interfere with their supply lines.

In addition, we are considering how railroads affect the government control of a province, city, or local area and also government influence on foreign countries. Although we are still brainstorming this, increased connectivity of your nation will likely mean both a greater flow of new ideas and means of enforcing the rule of law. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

In general, the mechanics of logistics are one of the foundations of Gilded Destiny, supporting higher-level mechanics such as trade and warfare. You will need to strike a delicate balance between maintenance costs and comprehensive benefits by carefully planning the distribution of land and water transport lines and upgrading the levels of your logistics buildings. When all is running smoothly in your logistics network, your whole country will thank you by running smoothly also.

notes.title: Dev Diary 2 - Buildings
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/2b98baec25acdc01913a6fc03d4d32acff8dc0cb.png[/img]

Hello everyone and welcome to the second dev diary for Gilded Destiny!

During the initial design process, we dedicated a significant amount of focus to shaping one of the most important parts of the game, as we see it—the buildings feature. Our methodology and current vision will be the topic of today's dev diary.

[h1]Production Buildings[/h1]
Since Gilded Destiny is partially an economic simulation, one of the primary aspects of the game is to construct production buildings to produce sufficient commodities so that farmers can support themselves and factory workers can produce enough valuable goods to help our economy industrialize.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/6d4841d75af2dadab569b0847154a1274f8b087c.png[/img]

Each production building will attempt to hire employees and maximize its income by automatically increasing or decreasing production unless you specifically set it to manual. You as the owner of the building (more on that later) can manually control what goods the building produces. For example, a slaughterhouse can adopt different production formulas and switch inputs from cattle to sheep. You can change the goods the building produces based on your region's comparative advantage and what would be most successful on the market.

Buildings will often have certain placement requirements. Farms must be built on arable hexagons and harbors must be built on a coastal hexagon. Building efficiency will depend on many variables such as terrain type and climate. For example, yields from crops located in colder regions will not be as high, while tropical regions are more suitable for cultivating fruit.

[h1Building Placement and ]Locality[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/5269b7ebe5cc11bfc565a73c1328330eea9c886d.png[/img]

The placement of buildings should be significant and will impact the surroundings just like in real life. We created a system to emulate this: Proximity Impact. The existence of buildings will have an impact on surrounding people and other buildings. For example, if we were to build a cement plant in the center of the city, the cement plant would produce a significant amount of pollution, reducing the happiness of the population living and working nearby. If your population's happiness goes too low, they will start to protest and this may lead to various effects such as a reduction in labor efficiency at your factories, causing a debuff on your tax collection efficiency, and may even outright foment a rebellion against you. On the other hand, placing complementary buildings together will likely be beneficial to the efficiency of both buildings—a shortened logistical chain will provide you with some extra bonus in productivity.

Just to clarify, unlike most grand strategy games, you can decide specifically where to place buildings on the map. We hope that the variety of building types with different functions plus the art of strategically placing buildings will make the game far more immersive and interesting.

[h1]Owners[/h1]

Every building has an owner. It can be built and owned by a capitalist, a nobleman, or by the state itself (i.e., you). The owner will need to pay the workers in production buildings, buy raw materials, and fulfill orders for profit. In short, the owner is responsible for the factory. 

At the start of the game, nobles will be your primary investors and provide funding for production buildings. Before the Industrial Revolution, the primary source of income for the nobility was land ownership. In the game, nobles will primarily focus on developing mining operations, agriculture, and to a lesser degree, factories.

Capitalists, on the other hand, primarily finance and own production buildings in cities. As you industrialize, you will see an increasingly influential capitalist class financing your economic growth. They will construct buildings within your country on their own, trying to produce a profit, and also making your job easier.

Buildings can also be state-owned. In such cases, you take direct control over the building. All profits and business expenses, including wages, will be billed directly to your National Budget. While having direct control of all production can theoretically give you an advantage, achieving such an advantage will not be easy. You will need to appoint qualified leaders, implement favorable policies, and most importantly, tediously adjust the intricacies of every factory you own to achieve profitability. Whether you can own buildings will depend on your national policies. You may have the option to seize production from others or be prevented from possesing state-owned buildings at all.

With our ownership design, we want to give you various choices for how to run your country. You can get directly involved with the management of each building to dictate what goods are being produced, or you can step back and let the market economy decide. You are in control (however, terms of your national economic policies will apply).

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/433c298ef8b493b5b75177f82c2e7a00b123cd81.png[/img]
(Here is a sneak peek of us testing road networks )

[h1]Other Buildings[/h1]

The last part for us to talk about is non-production buildings. There are a lot of buildings that are not production related, so we will not talk about them one by one. When we discuss each future system later, we will go deeper into them.

Most of the non-production buildings belong to the state and most will not be focused on profit-driven activities. For example, the Parliament building, national stock exchange, administrative buildings, railway stations, port terminals, and schools, etc. They all have their own functions and effects, and people are employed by them just like production buildings.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/aaf2ae4d5c8d3d15174e69767ad2929fc33759e0.png[/img]

Hopefully, after today's dev diary, you will have a better idea about how we envision the building system. In principle, we want players to be able to take more direct control when desired, yet able to rely on AI to automate most of it.

If you would like to keep up to date, wishlist us on Steam and follow us on Twitter and Facebook!

notes.title: Dev Diary 1 - Population
notes.content:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/75ab68fc68f0fd21a1bea116a7378923ac1442d9.png[/img]
Hello everyone! Today we will delve into one of Gilded Destiny's most defining and foundational features—Population. Please note many of the images shown below today came from our early design works. Final implementation in the game will very likely differ but will likely give you some good hints on where we are heading. Please enjoy it and let us know your feedback!

[h1]Vision for Population[/h1]
The population and its underlying societal change is a critical piece to the story of the industrial revolution. The population's ever-changing satisfaction, wealth, jobs, religions, cultures, and new ideas all serve as the drivers for change for a country's direction in the economy, military, and many other fields.

During the course of the 19th century, industrialization and technological breakthroughs brought about rapid societal changes. We saw an explosion in population and nations of agrarian societies transformed into industrialized ones. Countless subsistence farmers (yeomen) went from tending their own fields to workers in towering factories. While the Industrial Revolution represented incredible progress in wealth creation, education, and urbanization, it also brought about many tragedies—child labor, unsafe working conditions, unsanitary living conditions, and environmental pollution all plagued the era, from which we are still seeing the aftermath of today.

As the population became more skilled and educated, troves of new ideas also followed. Demand for better working conditions, desire for more social benefits, creation of institutions for higher learning, and the inception of political ideas such as Liberalism and Socialism all began during the era.

When a population is satisfied with their needs, they are the engine for a country's growth. They will establish more productive and efficient factories to create more tax revenue, join the military to conquer new lands, or pen  research to create new advancements. On the other hand, if they live in constant poverty, many will seek other jobs or migrate to find better opportunities elsewhere, while others will protest, organize strikes, or even join rebellions to overthrow the government.  

In summary, we see the population system as one of the core systems that will steer a nation's trajectory.

[h1]Population Groups[/h1]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/e5d8ca8482cf152b464b1ac669090907dfea7030.png[/img]
While we may all have the dream to one day create the ultimate simulation, to simulate all the possible details down to the individuals, it is unfortunately not possible for us to do with our current computer's performance envelope. (Maybe one day when we master quantum computers perhaps?) Therefore, grouping populations with similar attributes has become a necessity. 

In Gilded Destiny, every population group has its job, culture, religion, location, literacy rate, income and many qualities (more on that later).

Jobs is arguably the most important attribute for each population as it largely determines their wealth, needs and likely qualities. Currently, we have about 20 jobs in our game distributed across different societal levels. Each has their own behaviors, needs, and qualities.

[h1]Population Needs[/h1]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/2114a1accce13d3793024c24fd9261347c411c80.png[/img]
Depending on different attributes, such as jobs, culture, religions, or location of a population, their needs will differ. For example, educators will consume more books, aristocrats and capitalists will consume more luxury items, the population living in colder climates will require more wood or coal for warmth, and people from certain islands within Europe may have a certain fancy for tea.

Some needs are substitutable with a similar product if needed. When meat is scarce, the population may substitute it with grains, although it will incur a penalty in the required quantity. Coal may also be substituted with wood, for example.

Population needs and regional variations in production form the basis for logistics of goods flowing between regions and trade between countries. Now you have reasons to conquer new territories and optimize production; meanwhile, countries now have reasons to trade with one another.

However, when needs are not met, people will become rebellious and the nation will become unstable with uprisings popping up all over. Therefore, countries may also be pushed to war in order to acquire certain goods. Going to war over tea, anyone?

[h1]Population Qualities[/h1]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/3d9ba9f12ce0035a0db842478a18e3af47745636.png[/img]
A concept repeatedly mentioned above, "Quality," is one of the most important aspects of each population group. Each population group has a set of specific defining Qualities, which essentially act as traits in game that offer buffs or debuffs to the group.

Based on their jobs, culture, religion, education level, income level, and other factors, people will have different beliefs about their country and the world. These beliefs, in turn, will affect their actual behavior in game.

For example, Eastern cultures are influenced by Confucian Quality, and they are more collectivist in nature, which creates stronger social cohesion and willingness to tolerate more authoritarian rule. On the other hand, population groups with Western traditions are more likely to be influenced by Qualities that ensure that individual rights are guaranteed above all else and a more aggressive desire for democracy.

In addition to ideas about the state and politics, people also have different ideas about their lives and jobs, some groups are better at certain jobs, and some groups are more prone to rebellion. These are all realized in gameplay through Qualities.

However, the Qualities of a population are not set in stone and can be changed over time. Understanding and shaping the Qualities of your subject population will be a critical challenge for you as a leader. Qualities can be slowly shaped through events, initatives in provinces, national policies, and many others. Some qualities can also be gained or removed through special historical events. At times, in order to modernize your country and implement new policies, you may first need to sway or change the Qualities your population possesses in order to avoid a revolt. For example, this means that modernizing the Qing Empire will be a much tougher task than just putting people into factories. It will require the people to change their views and ideas first.

[h1]Modding[/h1]
Players can adjust the initial distribution of the population in each region, the overall education level, and even add more jobs, cultures, and religious types. Adjusting these parameters affects the type and quantity of needs, their qualities, and the overall birth rate and death rate of the population.

All of the above is done through a built-in editor in the game. The editor will also have a population group generation tool that allows you to tweak population-wide parameters, such as job distribution, and it will generate all the underlying population groups for you. This should allow you to make quick changes to populations without physically editing every single pop.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The population system is fundamental to the entire game, affecting almost every other feature of the game, and yet also heavily affected by other features. Today, we have only scratched the surface of the population feature. However, fear not, we will have more details relating to other features in future Dev Diaries!

If you have any questions, also please feel free to comment below!

Here is a bonus image of our full population mockup:
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/43221501/5c36b11ff989c97186d49af3456a8b2ff5dce53b.png[/img]
